How Fintechs Should Choose Their Next Growth Move Maxine P. 4 min read · Sep 22, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Among 4,658 current or prospective crypto users surveyed across 15 countries, 77% said they would open a stablecoin wallet if their primary bank or fintech app offered one. That points to a broader product question. When a fintech wants its next growth vector, the usual options are obvious: enter another country, target another segment, launch a partnership or spend more on acquisition. All of them expand distribution. But growth can also come from the opposite direction — giving the users already inside the product more reasons to use it. The two strategies solve different constraints. If the problem is reach, the company needs more users. If users are already there but repeatedly leave the product for adjacent financial services, the opportunity may be product depth instead. How to Tell Which Issue You Actually Have A new market usually means building demand and distribution around a different audience. A new use case starts from an audience the company already understands. That does not automatically make the second route easier or cheaper. An unused feature can be just as expensive as a failed acquisition campaign. The stronger signal is behavioral leakage : customers are already trying to complete a financial job, but they have to leave your product to do it. A practical framework could look like this: Press enter or click to view image in full size That is a more useful distinction than “new users VS loyal users.” The question is where the unserved demand already exists . Fintechs can find those signals in outbound transfers, connected accounts, support requests, waitlists, transaction patterns and customer research. And some adjacent services are naturally easier to test than others: investing, cross-border payments, savings products and digital assets all extend financial relationships users already have. Crypto Shows How One Feature Can Serve Two Growth Goals Crypto is particularly interesting because the same capability can work on both sides of the equation. - For an existing customer, it can keep another financial activity inside the app: buying an asset, holding stablecoins or transferring crypto without moving money to another platform. - For a prospective customer, the same functionality can become another reason to choose the fintech in the first place. There is already evidence that this behavior is moving into embedded products. BVNK reports that stablecoin-wallet volume on its platform increased 263x year over year , with PSPs and fintechs responsible for 75% of that volume . But the distinction matters operationally: If crypto is meant primarily to activate existing users , product teams should look for evidence that those users already perform the activity elsewhere. If it is meant primarily to acquire new users , the feature has to be strong enough to influence platform choice in a crowded market. And if neither condition is true, adding crypto infrastructure will not manufacture product-market fit. Once the Demand Exists, the Infrastructure Question Changes At that point, the decision becomes less about whether to offer crypto and more about how much of the stack the fintech wants to build and operate itself . There is no single model: Bitpanda Enterprise takes a broad investment-platform approach: Its infrastructure combines 650+ crypto assets with 10,000+ stocks, ETFs, metals and commodities , making it relevant when crypto is part of a larger investing proposition rather than a standalone feature. WhiteBIT Crypto-as-a-Service is structured as a white-label crypto layer: Businesses can integrate wallet creation, storage, buying and selling, deposits and withdrawals under their own brand — within 4 weeks. And from Day 1, launch with 340+ crypto and fiat assets across 80+ networks . Zero Hash sits further in the backend: It supports 100+ assets across 200 jurisdictions , already powering millions of end customers — providing trading, liquidity, custody and compliance while fintech keeps control of the customer experience. These approaches solve different versions of the same problem. One company may want a broad investment catalogue. Another may want infrastructure hidden almost entirely behind its own interface. A third may need a dedicated crypto product without building custody, liquidity and asset connectivity from zero. That is why provider selection should come after the growth thesis is clear. Growth Can Come From Reach or Depth Entering a new market, launching partnerships and opening new acquisition channels are still valid ways to grow. But they should not be the automatic response every time a fintech needs its next revenue line. Sometimes the stronger signal is already inside the customer base: users are active, but part of their financial activity is happening somewhere else. The useful sequence is therefore: Find the missing behavior → validate that it is recurring → decide whether capturing it improves the customer relationship → only then choose the infrastructure.
